chapter: Touring shows and the bands he heard
title: Learning chord sounds and playing ad-lib by ear
summary: He traces the minor seventh flat-five sound back to Mississippi and explains he learned chords rather than copying records.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Many kind of ways I learned lessons, you know. I was listening to Dizzy on the review one day, on the radio, Dizzy Gillespie, and he was saying how he learned about the minor seventh with the flat five in it; he learned it from Thelonious Monk in New York, and that's what they got together on the introduction to "Round About Midnight," you know. But I remember coming in contact with that chord back home. Because my cousin lived with us, and she was studying piano. Not that she wanted to; because the family wanted her to. She was playing the piano... She was taking piano lessons, you know, and she had books. And I'd fool around in her book a little bit now and then to see what...you know, look at the piano book and fool around at the piano. And I ran into this sound that they call the minor seven

with the flat five. And then I heard Robert E. Lee wrote it on "Indian Love Call" for the band one time, Don Dunbar's band, and they called it C-minor sixth with A in the bass -- which is the same thing. You see? So I was familiar with that sound way back in Mississippi.

I was aware of that sound, you know, because I had studied the chords, and I knew my chords very well. By the time I got to fourteen years old, I could play chords upside-down, back and around again, because that's the way I learned to play -- ad-lib. I didn't learn like most kids learned, by listening to the records or copping the solos off there, even though I liked things and I listened to the records. But I never copied anything off the record until this day. Not that that's really good, because you're playing by ear by copying. But I imagine it works out.

I learned the chords, and I usually could transpose the chords to my alto saxophone as fast as the piano player called them to me. Like, we'd play a dance or something. If I didn't know something, just call me the chords. I'd just run up and down them. Until eventually, I learned how to make them make sense, you know. And in time, I learned to hear them. I trained my ear that way. So I imagine it works out. But it was the way that I learned how to play -- ad-lib solos.
